The breeding biology of the Horned lark (Eremophila alpestris) is characterized by a moderately high reproductive output for a passerine of its size. During a typical breeding season, females lay clutches of about 2.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = about 2.5 eggs per clutch], which represents a standard fecundity for ground-nesting alaudids. Many individuals will attempt up to three nesting cycles over the course of a single season, leading to a frequency of three clutches per year [F_R_i = three clutches per year]. This intensive reproductive schedule is facilitated by the species' occupation of open, often arid habitats where the growing season for insect prey is relatively short but productive under favorable thermal conditions. Indeed, these values were obtained from a population studied when ambient conditions averaged 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], reflecting the hot, sun-exposed environments this lark typically inhabits. The energetic demands of producing and incubating multiple clutches are considerable, and females must maintain high foraging rates to sustain egg formation and subsequent provisioning of the altricial nestlings.

Hatchling Horned larks emerge from the egg after a development period of 12 days [ab = 12 days] when incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This incubation duration is consistent with that of other small, open-cup nesting passerines. At the moment of hatching, the neonates are altricial and weigh a mere 2.73 grams [Wwb = 2.73 grams], a mass that represents only a small fraction of the eventual adult size. The egg from which they hatch is somewhat heavier than the hatchling itself, with a fresh egg weight of approximately 2.9 grams, reflecting the considerable yolk and albumen reserves required to sustain the embryo through the full incubation period. Upon emergence, the newly hatched chick is entirely dependent on its parents for both warmth and nourishment, beginning a rapid phase of mass gain that characterizes the early nestling stage. The difference between the hatchling weight and the egg weight underscores the metabolic costs incurred during development, including the loss of water and the consumption of yolk stores.

Under the typical thermal conditions experienced by active adult Horned larks in their breeding territories, which often exceed 40 °C during the hottest part of the day, the developmental progression from hatching to independence follows a tightly constrained schedule. At 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a temperature that closely matches the species' preferred microclimate during foraging and nesting activities, a predictable sequence of life-history milestones unfolds. Fledging occurs at 9.1 days after hatching [tx = 9.1 days after hatching], a notably short nestling period that is characteristic of many open-country birds that face high predation risk on the ground at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Once the young leave the nest, they are still dependent on parental care for some time, but the risk of mortality is somewhat reduced as they can escape predators by running and, shortly thereafter, by making short flights. The rapid attainment of this developmental stage is a critical adaptation for survival in exposed habitats.

Sexual maturity in the Horned lark is attained relatively early in life when compared to many other passerines of similar body mass. Puberty is reached at 27.3 days after hatching [tp = 27.3 days after hatching] under the elevated thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] typical of their active season. This remarkably swift maturation is likely an adaptation to short, unpredictable breeding seasons in variable environments, allowing young birds hatched early in the season to potentially contribute to later nesting attempts within the same year. The first successful brood for a breeding individual, however, is often deferred until the following breeding season. Field records indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days] when measured at the same ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay, despite the early attainment of gonadal maturity, is probably related to the need for young birds to acquire necessary foraging skills and establish a territory.

The ultimate body mass attained by adult Horned larks reflects their adaptation to a relatively harsh and energetically demanding lifestyle. The adult asymptotic wet weight for this species is 33.8 grams [Wwi = 33.8 grams], a value that places Eremophila alpestris among the smaller members of the Alaudidae family. This modest size is associated with a relatively fast pace of life, as reflected in the species' maximal longevity. The maximum recorded lifespan for a Horned lark under natural conditions is 10 years [am = 10 years] when assessed at a metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Achieving this age is exceptional, as most individuals likely succumb to predation, starvation, or environmental extremes within their first few years. The combination of a low adult body mass, a high reproductive rate involving multiple small clutches per season, and a short generation time is a classic profile of a species adapted to unpredictable and often resource-poor environments.
